speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NATO AND NORAD-CONSIDERATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AS TO POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister a question relating to the desire of the members of the standing committee on external affairs and national defence to hold discussions in some depth with the ministers concerned regarding future defence and foreign policy. I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he will assure the house that before any definite decisions are taken regarding a change in defence policy, specifically with regard to NATO and NORAD, the committee will have an opportunity to consider and to make recommendations on the course of policy.
29180-194}

subtopic: NATO AND NORAD-CONSIDERATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AS TO POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand there will be a meeting of the committee on December 3 when these questions can be discussed. I would further hope that at some time in parliament, on a supply day or otherwise, we will have an occasion to discuss the whole question of external affairs and defence policies.
As I indicated several times, the government has asked for this review because we want Canada to have the best policy for the times. We do not feel we can find it by any magic process. We can do it only by consultation. I would hope there would be consultation not only of experts but of those particular experts called members of parliament in debate. I still have no idea concerning the timing of this report or at what date it will come forward to the government. Therefore I cannot make any specific commitment as to when that will be debated.
I do want to assure members of this house, however, that we will not reach any policy through a device which has bypassed parliament or indeed public opinion. We do want to arrive at a policy which will represent a good policy for Canada and which will have been discussed at all levels of public opinion.

In view of the potentially serious effect in our system of parliamentary government of the right hon. gentleman's decision to establish a series of regional offices and a body of 150 extraparliamentary advisers, would the Prime Minister at an early date make a statement on motions as to the duties and responsibilities of these new groups?

maintopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO ESTABLISH OUTSIDE ADVISORY GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel I should make a statement on motions, but I could by way of a short explanation indicate that these regional desk officers are in no way intended to compete with members of parliament. They are merely to provide an additional source of information to me as to what might be happening in various parts of the country. These persons in the regional desks have no legislative role and therefore they are perhaps more free to move around the country and to have access to people at times when members of parliament are held here in Ottawa. These desk officers will also be processing information from members of parliament to give to me. Therefore there is no intention to compete but merely to supplement members of parliament. There could be, of course, no competition anyhow because members of parliament are so far ahead in the political game.
As to the other part of the question, these people who have volunteered to take part in the process of constant evaluation of the performance of the government represent persons who have offered to let my office know of their assessment of the reaction in various parts of the country to things happening in Ottawa. speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply, revised estimates of the Department of Transport for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1969. Vote No. 1 will be found at page 496 of the blue book; the details thereof are listed at page 501. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, in presenting the estimates of the Department of Transport I feel it might be helpful and useful to take a few minutes of the committees' time to give hon. members some general explanations in respect of the more important areas of activity in the Department of Transport, particularly in relation to where substantial expenditures are necessary. I propose to deal with the main estimates of the department first and to confine my remarks to them.
It will be of interest to note that the form of the estimates for 1968-69 is somewhat different from that of previous years. One of the recommendations of the Glassco commission, as approved by the government, was that:
-where appropriate (i.e. where revenues are sufficiently large in proportion to the total vote to justify it) revenues be offset against related expenditures in individual votes: in such cases votes to be shown in the estimates and controlled on a net basis.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
After serious consideration of the many factors involved, not the least of which was that in 1968-69 we expect departmental revenues to exceed $48 million, we decided that we had reached the point where we should give effect to this recommendation. You will note, therefore, that votes 5 and 30 which provide funds for administration, operation and maintenance of marine services and of
November 22, 1963

air services, respectively, have this year been treated on the basis suggested by the Glassco commission, i.e., with the applicable revenues deducted from the gross total of expenditures to arrive at the net amount to be voted. We believe this manner of treatment of departmental revenues will be more informative.
In the year when such a change is first made it results in showing amounts which are not strictly comparable with those of the previous year when voting was on a gross basis, but this is only a one-time effect and will not be a factor in future years. We considered the possibility of showing the revenues of the previous year in the new manner in order to provide an exact basis of comparison, but this was found to be impossible because the previous year's figures would then no longer have indicated the amount actually voted by parliament. Nevertheless, if reference is made to the details of the estimates it will be found that there are listed, by sub-votes, both the revenues and expenditures of the past three years.
In dealing first with the marine services of the department I would like to report that the Canadian Coast Guard is involved in the annual sealift of northern supplies for government posts and installations in the Arctic. The tonnage involved is approximately 100,000, of which something less than half is for military installations. It is departmental policy that as far as possible supplies for the Arctic shall be carried by chartered ships with coast guard support confined to icebreaker and escort, and the provision of specialized landing craft which are not commercially available. An increase in estimated expenditure over last year is attributed to increases in charter rates, costs of stevedoring services and ship operating costs generally as well as some increase in the scope of our icebreaker activities.
Cost of operating coast guard lights and buoy tenders have risen some $74,000, due entirely to increases in wages, materials and supplies. The increase has been modified slightly by the substitution of one ship, the C.C.G.S. Bernier for two old vessels in the Quebec agency.
The Canadian organization for marine search and rescue is based on the use of all available resources under the general co-ordination of the Department of National Defence. In practice, the Department of Transport has a major role in marine search and rescue, as it has the largest fleet of government vessels, through its responsibility for the provision of
Supply-Transport
specialized craft and through the use of the D.O.T. communications network. An increase in estimates for this activity of some $200,000 is accounted for in part by an increasing commitment as a result of the larger number of small pleasure craft in our waters and greater public demand for this service as well as the first steps toward the acquisition of new craft under a program announced earlier.
The increase also reflects the acquisition of a hovercraft for operation on the west coast.
The department operates a service for the support of shipping in the gulf and lower St. Lawrence in winter consisting of aerial ice reconnaissance for the acquisition of information about ice conditions and an ice office in Halifax for interpretation and forecasting operated by the meteorological branch, ice information offices for the provision of information and advice to ships, and icebreaking. In addition, icebreaking is done in coastal fishing harbours, in support of some ferries and for flood control in the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. In general it is the department's policy to break ice only in the main shipping routes and approach channels, the responsibility for basins and water alongside wharves being left to their owners, except in the case of government-owned wharves.
Cost increases are partly due to general increases in the cost of ship operations, and partly the result of a growing demand for icebreaking brought about by the realization that the movement of commerce through our ice-congested waters in winter is perfectly practicable with the use of suitably strengthened merchant ships. The increase in winter trade in our waters has been spectacular in the last few years, and although it has slowed down it is expected that the long term trend will be toward continued increase.
Canada has responsibility by international agreement for the operation of an ocean weather station in the Pacific and this is undertaken by two coast guard vessels. The estimate for the operation of these craft shows a reduction from last year which was a transitional period between the use of old vessels and their replacement by the larger modern vessels Vancouver and Quadra. During the period of transition it was necessary to keep all four ships in operation while the new ones did trials and work-ups, but this period is over and the older ships are being disposed of.
The department maintains a college for the training of junior officers for the Canadian

November 22. 1968
Supply-Transport
Coast Guard. The college is also to be used for refresher and specialist training of older officers. The college now inhabits converted temporary wartime buildings formerly occupied by the navy at Point Edward, Nova Scotia, and the estimates include a provision toward the acquisition of a permanent establishment.
Improvements recently introduced in the marine traffic control system in the St. Lawrence river below Montreal will be assessed during the coming year and, except for some improvement in the radio communication facilities, 1969 will be considered as a period of consolidation for both equipment and procedures. Traffic control, with its attendant information services, will continue to extend gradually westward during the coming years in accordance with previously announced plans for an integrated system throughout the St. Lawrence waterway. Improvements in up to date methods of data collection, transmission, display and dissemination will continue in marine information services.
The widening of the ship channel through lake St. Peter began in 1969. When this project is completed, the minimum width of the channel will be 800 ft. throughout. Widening of this 20-mile long channel will take three years to complete at a cost of $7,500,000. The allotment for 1968-69 is $2 million. A project is at present under way to improve the north channel below Quebec. This is the only remaining section of the St. Lawrence ship channel not dredged to the statutory depth of 35 feet. This north channel work replaces the proposed plan to deepen the south channel in the same region to the same depth of 35 feet. Representations by the Pilots' Association, and a subsequently higher estimated cost to bring the south channel to prescribed standards, were instrumental in postponing the south channel project indefinitely. An amount of $2,139,000 has been allotted to the dredging below Quebec for 1968-69.
In the interest of safe navigation, work continued in 1968 on the removal of a midriver shoal at Trois-Rivieres. The 1968-69 allotment is $2,165,000.
Experimental ice booms and islands were placed in lake St. Peter in the fall of 1967 to develop a means to prevent ice from drifting into the main channel. The success of this experiment to date warrants its continuation in 1968-69. The allotment for 1968 is $525,000, to cover the cost of improving the ice boom system and artificial ice retention islands.

An amount of $300,000 is provided for the construction of a pilot boat to be based at Prince Rupert where it will replace a wooden boat which has come to the end of its useful life after 35 years.
[DOT] (12 noon)
Funds are provided to establish a maritime safety council, which would be a consultative body representative of government, management and labour in the commercial shipping industry, for the purpose of advising the Department of Transport on all matters of safety relating to commercial ships and vessels, at an estimated annual cost of $50,000.
Funds are also provided for the construction of 44-foot shore-based lifeboats, various barges and other small craft; also funds to cover research and development toward the construction of better and more efficient vessels to serve the Canadian public.
To increase safety on the St. Lawrence river and extend the navigation season $1.2 million has been provided for the construction of new offshore piers that will provide navigational lights.
Navigation throughout Canada will benefit from the construction of lighthouse buildings, light towers, fog alarms and fog alarm buildings which, together with the cost of equipment required to service these aids, represent an expenditure of approximately $4.5 million.
There are several items of significance in the air services. They include in the airports activity the takeover from municipal governments of the operation of airports at Saint John, New Brunswick, and House Harbour, Quebec, the complete operation of Goose airport for a full year for the first time, and the opening and operation of the new air terminal at Vancouver international airport which commenced operation in September. In the control of civil aviation funds have been provided for a new flight safety division which will permit a more vigorous compaign on air safety practices and accident prevention.
In air traffic control an accelerated program continues for recruiting and training controllers. Funds for five additional control towers are provided in the estimates and it is planned to provide each air services region with one mobile control tower for temporary control services as the need arises.
Funds for the telecommunications bureau and administration bureau, formerly included in air services accounts, now appear under
November 22, 1968

the Post Office Department in the main estimates and this results in a subsequent net reduction of $3,431,000 in air services expenditures.
In meteorological services additional funds are budgeted for new weather observing programs to be undertaken by contract ($200,000), increasing the number of ice reconnaissance flights ($140,000), and an extended program for fellowships and contracts with universities for research studies ($90,000). The estimates also include necessary funds for the transfer of the annual airlift of supplies for Arctic weather stations from the Canadian armed forces to commercial carriers at a cost of $100,000.
Funds are included for the acquisition and construction of complex facilities to serve the rapid development of air transport. Some of the major projects include the construction of a new area control centre at Vancouver international airport ($1,300,000), and the construction of a low level bridge across the middle arm of the Fraser river to improve access to that airport ($825,000), the start of construction on a second air terminal at Toronto international airport and a substantial program to improve existing terminals at Montreal and Calgary.
Special centre line and touchdown lighting, scheduled for major main line airports over the next five years, will be installed at Montreal and Vancouver international airports, costing $300,000 for each installation. These lighting systems will improve the frequency and safety of landings in very poor weather conditions. Provision is made for a start in the development of a main line airport to serve the Churchill Falls development, for a start in the redevelopment of the airport at Matane, Quebec, and for starts of runway improvements at Fort Chimo, Schefferville, Red Lake, Inuvik and Norman Wells. Experience has shown that work of this nature cannot be completed in one construction season. An amount of $600,000 is provided to acquire land for the development of a satellite airport at Calgary for light aircraft in order to prevent the volume of traffic exceeding the capacity of the main airport serving that city. An amount of $300,000 is also provided for further development of the satellite airport serving Winnipeg.
A number of special projects are planned to advance our techniques in the control of air traffic by the use of radar. These include a secondary surveillance radar system which will greatly enhance the amount of flight
Supply-Transport
information which can be sent electronically from the aircraft to the ground controller ($1,450,000); new techniques will be developed in the display of radar data and its conversion to electronic signals which will be adaptable to computer use ($350,000); and the continuation of improvement of radar displays so that they can be monitored under daylight conditions ($474,000). A program of improving instrument landing systems at major airports to meet new international standards is entering the third year of an eight year $5 million program.
With respect to railway and ferry services the introduction of the new rail car ferry Frederick Carter for the major portion of 1968 will result in a decrease from past years' cost on the Cabot strait ferry service. A new ferry service running between North Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Argentia, Newfoundland, commenced operation on June 14, 1968.
The construction program for terminals and vessels on ferry services has decreased considerably as a result of completion of the main facilities and vessels. The federal government has now taken over direct responsibility for provident fund deficits.
The proposed new road and motor vehicle safety office to be established in the department has been delayed somewhat because of the over-all government financial restrictions. It is expected, however, that the staff for this safety office will be recruited shortly and the office will become operational by the end of 1968. Following formation of the safety office a public advisory board will also be created.
In addition to the estimates of the Department of Transport I am submitting those of the National Harbours Board. The capital expenditures proposed for this agency aggregate $29,172,000, of which $5,022,000 will be financed from its replacement and other funds.
The major items in the construction program to be undertaken by the board contemplate expenditures of $11,394,000 for wharf construction and acquisition, $2,546,000 for shed construction and renovation, $2,390,000 for elevator construction and renovation, $5,-
800,000	for property acquisitions and site development, $2,235,000 for provision of facilities for container handling, $722,000 for renovation and construction of buildings, $304,000 for paving harbour properties, $340,000 for harbour railway extensions, $155,000 for patrol and work vessels, $2,000,000 for St. Charles river project, Quebec-construction of retaining walls, $425,000 for underground

November 22, 1988
Supply-Transport
services, sewer installation and replacement of electric sub-station, and $225,000 for replacement of electrical equipment-grain elevator system.
If I may I would now like to refer to the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. As of November 14, 1968, bulk cargoes were up by 8 per cent on the Montreal-Lake Ontario section and by 7 per cent on the Welland section, compared with the same period in 1967. General cargoes increased by 32 per cent on the Montreal-Lake Ontario section and by 40 per cent on the Welland section, compared with the same period last year. Total traffic is 11.6 per cent more on the Montreal-Lake Ontario section and 10.5 per cent more on the Welland than during the same period in 1967. The increase in bulk cargoes took place notwithstanding the seaway strike and a decreased flow of grain from the lakehead. The increase in general cargoes is due mainly to a substantial increase in the movement of manufactured iron and steel.
The 1967 navigation season marked the first full year of operation of the new traffic control centre on the Welland canal. This traffic control system, which had become operational in the summer of 1966, was expanded during the non-navigation season of 1966-67 to include the lock and harbour areas of the canal. The procedure, which includes the use of closed circuit television and telemetry, has improved the scheduling of vessels through the canal and has resulted in substantial reductions in lock cycle and round trip transit times.
The techniques and experience gained on the Welland are being applied gradually in the eastern region, with certain refinements. The first step in this project was the installation of new traffic lights and a surveillance system at the Beauharnois lock, as well as modernization of the Beauharnois traffic control centre. This became fully operational in 1968.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Work continued in 1967 and early 1968 at the Cote Ste. Catherine and St. Lambert locks to provide a better control of icing conditions during the critical closing and opening periods of the seaway each year. These works include ice diversion channels and ice flushing culverts at both locks and an enlargement of the regulating works at the Cote Ste. Catherine lock.
The seaway authority announced in March of this year that the Lachine and Cornwall

canals would be closed to navigation permanently at the end of the 1968 season. These shallow draft canals, once important links in the old St. Lawrence canals system, have become increasingly uneconomic in the face of rising operating costs and diminishing traffic resulting from the opening of the seaway in 1959. The 11 million tons carried by these canals in 1958 had decreased by 1967 to
338,000	tons on the Lachine and 100,000 on the Cornwall.
Although the closing will not necessarily affect the water supply and drainage facilities of local industries, the maintenance of such conveniences will, of course, become much more costly. Accordingly, the availability of a cheaper alternative is under study, and the matter will be reverted to when the study and consultations with interested municipalities and industries have been completed. Work continued in 1968 on the construction of a new channel to bypass the city of Welland. Settlement has been reached with about 83.6 per cent of the owners of the 4,000 acres of land expropriated for this purpose. Clearing of the right of way is essentially complete. Five major contracts have been awarded for about 5.93 miles of the total 8.3 miles of excavation required. By the end of 1968 contracts covering channel excavations for approximately 7.28 miles out of the over-all total length of 8.3 miles of the Welland by pass should be under active construction. Approximately 23 per cent of the required total channel excavation for the Welland bypass was completed as of August 31, 1968.
The year 1968-69 represents the first full year of operation of the Canadian Transport Commission which came into being pursuant to the proclamation of part I of the National Transportation Act last fall. While still undergoing the process of organization, the regulatory aspects of the commission's operations, to the extent authorized by the legislation thus far proclaimed, are proceeding in a normal manner and represent to a large extent a continuation of those functions carried out by the commission's predecessor agencies.
In keeping with the government's policy of maintaining the highest possible level of commercial air services in regional areas, the air transport committee has initiated an increasing number of examinations of regional requirements during the past year. For example, public hearings of this nature were undertaken in the maritimes, Manitoba, Yellowknife and Frobisher Bay and resulting decisions have been issued or are under current examination.
November 22, 1968



The railway transport committee has received and is dealing with some 160 applications relating to the abandonment of non-guaranteed branch lines, discontinuance of railway passenger train service, the removal of railway station agents and caretakers, and applications for the inauguration of master agency and customer service plans of the major railways. In addition the committee has recently conducted a public hearing designed to produce uniform costing procedures to be used by Canadian railways which will ensure that at all times the commission and the railways will use proper costing methods and that cost figures submitted by the railways or determined by the commission will be correct and acceptable for the purposes of the Railway Act.
During the past year over $26 million has been committed from the railway grade crossing fund to provide assistance to municipalities in meeting the costs of constructing or reconstructing 67 railway-highway grade separations, 11 diversions, and the installation or improvement of automatic protection facilities at 544 railway-highway crossings. In accordance with the provisions of the National Transportation Act relating to the gradual reduction in subsidies to railway and transportation companies, it will be noted that a decrease of $14 million has been made in the provision of the estimates now before the house, which reflects the first of the annual decreases established.
In the early part of the year the water transport committee completed the public hearings stage of the inquiry into the ownership and registration of ships in Canada. The committee's report is in the process of preparation and is expected to be completed shortly.
In accordance with the provisions of the National Transportation Act a research division has been created within the commission. In addition, an advisory council on research, comprising informed Canadians outside of government, has been established to assist in developing a research program and assigning priorities within it. The forecasting of transportation supply and demand and the undertaking of broad cost-benefit studies in the transportation area will be central to the research program.
The estimates for the Canadian Transport Commission, the National Harbours Board and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority have been referred to the parliamentary committee on transportation, while the estimates of the
Supply-Transport
department are being dealt with before the house. Indeed, I understand that the parliamentary committee is meeting today on these subjects. For that reason, in response to any questions from hon. members I propose to limit my comments or answers to matters concerning the department only, since questions relating to these other agencies should be raised and can be answered in the parliamentary committee where special witnesses are available for this purpose.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. At this time I should like to make a suggestion to the committee. Further to the concluding remarks of the minister, the committee will notice that items 45 and L 115 dealing with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are part of the estimates of the Minister of Transport. If there is general agreement, I believe it possibly would be in the interests of orderly procedure if we were to avoid a discussion of these items because they are before a standing committee. We might concentrate in committee of supply on the transportation items alone.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we are in agreement with the exclusion of the housing item from the discussion, but in so far as these other matters are concerned which are before committees I feel we are entitled to mention them where policy is concerned particularly when the minister, so far as I know, has made no full statement before the committee. The first proviso, however, is valid so far as we are concerned.
May I say we are very pleased to have the comprehensive report the minister has given us. I believe it is one of the first concrete moves he has made to show he is interested in transport. Once or twice I almost detected a faint glimmer of pride when he was outlining the new and extensive activities of his department. The hon. member for Oxford is our chief spokesman in matters of transport and he has dealt extensively with this subject in the committee and in the house from time to time. I am really pinchhitting for him. If the minister understands anything about the navy he will realize that I have been taken out of mothballs to say something on these estimates today.
I recall that when the former minister, Mr. Pickersgill, left he made this announcement which has been mentioned in the house previously: "I am leaving the department. It is in great shape. My job has been completed. I have finished the great work in transport." Yet simultaneously in another interview the

November 22, 1968
Supply-Transport
present minister said: "I consider this the greatest challenge of my life; the department is in such a mess." Of course, in thinking the minister might be right one is tempted to ask the rhetorical question, what kind of a mess is the Canadian Transport Commission now in with Mr. Pickersgill as its new head? I do not know who is right in this argument, but I do suggest that the department is a tremendously complex one which affects all walks of life in Canada.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
I pay tribute to the minister in that I think he has the energy and capacity to tackle the problems facing transport. He did so in respect of national defence. I do not agree with what he did and I said so in the house, but if he puts his mind to these problems I think he has the capacity and has demonstrated that he can use it. I hasten to place on the record that transport has been sadly neglected while the minister has been galavanting about the country on his housing foray which has so far shown little success. We recognized long before the government that housing has a definite priority, but I wonder what is happening to his giant department while the minister is piloting this inquiry.
I cannot help but use nautical expressions when I think of the minister wiping out the navy. He seems to want to assume command and be the pilot. This is about the only nautical action in connection with transport that the minister has taken since assuming his present portfolio. In any event Mr. Pickersgill has left-I will deal with him later-and the present minister is at the helm. But all we have, as has been stated many times in this house, is a lot of unfinished business.
First of all, I think of the various reports and surveys which have been coming up so fast in this department. Many of them have been requested by members on this side of the house, but where are these reports? I have not had the chance to deal extensively with them and I do not know the state of them. This is one of the reasons we want the minister in the house, so he can deal with the problems of transport on a day to day basis and give us up to date information. We do not know, for example, the state of affairs concerning the marine branch of the minister's department. What is happening in respect of the Canada Shipping Act? We know something is to be done in this regard but we have not heard anything about it.

The pilotage report was completed, and I agree with many of its recommendations, but how are these being treated by the department? The minister has not said anything in that regard. We also have the National Harbours Board report. I understand the minister fell asleep over the week end while reading it. We do not know the position with respect to that report. The merchant navy has been under study on three occasions in recent years that I can remember. Promises were made during the election campaign in this regard. They have been referred to in the house, but what has the government done? It is going to conduct another study, but the difference is that this one is to be in depth. I hope we do not have to go through all these other studies and start new ones in depth.
The Canadian shipbuilding industry is floundering. What is the government doing in this regard? What is taking place in respect of containers? One of the officers of the transport commission said the other day that within a few weeks another research study would be conducted on containerization. We have many problems in respect of ferries, at least in the maritimes, and they are still up in the air.
I have only dealt thus far with the marine situation, but what is happening in respect of air transport? The minister told us about the many new plans the department has in so far as air transport is concerned. I should like the minister when he replies to tell us what the position is of the Wheatcroft report, the Robinson report and the Thompson report. Those are three I can think of right now without looking anything up, and there may be many more. What is happening to the new plans for airport development to accommodate the new jumbo jets?
We must not forget the rail transportation system. There have been all kinds of promises in this regard, and these promises have been indelibly recorded in this house. The former minister stood up when we were passing the National Transportation Act and said that the government would deal with the problems facing the maritimes if the house would only let that bill go through. We did so but these problems have not even been reported on. How about the changes in the Maritime Freight Rates Act? What is happening in respect of l.c.l. business? There have been so many reports on this subject I cannot keep them straight. They have been passed on to the provincial governments which have in turn passed them back to Ottawa. We must
November 22, 1968



pay attention to those regions of Canada which were left out when the new National Transportation Act was passed.
Many other matters dealing with different facets of transportation have also been postponed. I understand that the entire responsibility in respect of satellites has been turned over to the new Postmaster General. Perhaps that is a good thing. However, I do not know where these reports are. I hope the new Minister of Transport received them when he took over. I have referred to about ten of them. Are they lying around in the minister's office or did Mr. Pickersgill take them with him? Perhaps they are in the reading room of the Rideau Club. I want to know where these reports are and I want an up to date review. Let us know what is happening.
This brings up the question of who is really the boss in respect of transportation in this country. Is it the minister or is it the new chief dictator of the Canadian Transport Commission? One of them is relaxing and holding cabinet meetings-small ones, I must admit-at the Rideau Club each day. On the other hand we have an itinerant traveller in the person of the minister himself running about the country. Who is running this department and who is the real boss? Is it pious Paul or sailor Jack who is running this *department?
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Yes.

My friend has talked about the itinerant minister. He is referring to one of the most senior cabinet members in the government. Does he not think that part of the duties of the Minister of Transport is to travel about and find out what is going on in this country so that he can assess these problems and their effects on this nation? Does he not think this requires a diligent inquiry?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
The minister is travelling
throughout the country but we would prefer him to be in the house on the days he is supposed to be here, which are few enough as it is. We also think he should pay some attention to transportation as well as to housing. Let me take this opportunity to say something about the outrageous attendance roster for ministers which has been initiated. I see that the understudy to the Minister of Transport is in the house and I am glad he is here. I think I am paying him the biggest compliment I can by suggesting he is the type of man who
Supply-Transport
would be in the house every day of the week if only the Prime Minister would allow him to be here on those days he is not supposed to be here.
I have referred to the czar of the transport commission who holds meetings at the Rideau Club. I think he feels the weight of his responsibilities a little and that on many occasions when he holds these meetings and begins to stick out his chest he feels he is really still the minister of transport. Mr. Pickersgill was discovered at a meeting in Halifax on November 9. I know there has been some denial in the press in this regard, but I suggest there must have been something going on in view of the fact the minister said, as reported in a Halifax newspaper:
Hon. J. W. Pickersgill said in Halifax during the week end he has confidential information to back up the statement.
The statement was that Halifax will be the likely choice as the eastern container terminal. I am not quarrelling in respect of Halifax v. Saint John, as we are friendly rivals in this regard, but I do not think the head of the transport commission has any business making statements which would indicate that he prefers Halifax over Saint John.

Would you settle for Halifax, then?
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
This is what we are up against when we talk of transportation. I hope the minister will continue to stand up on his own two feet and be proud of his department. I hope he will accept all his responsibilities. Let us have full cabinet meetings to decide on solutions to transportation problems. Never mind these little meetings in the Rideau Club over lunch.
Another matter I want to refer to concerns the National Harbours Board. Its estimates are being dealt with in committee, as the minister has said. I only want to reiterate what I said the other day, that the National Harbours Board has in my opinion been very fair in the past in its treatment of all Canadian ports that come under its jurisdiction. I have no quarrel with the way it has acted in this regard. Many of us feel the National Harbours Board might have done more, but I do not think there is any allegation that it has given preferential treatment to one port over another.
However, a situation has developed in the eastern Canadian ports which requires that

November 22, 1968
Supply-Transport
the National Harbours Board continue to be scrupulously lair with regard to providing facilities or advantages to each of the ports. We dealt with this question yesterday. I simply say that in connection with rail transportation rates in and out of these ports, and also the most important matter of wharfage costs, there should not be hidden benefits or advantages to any port. We have every confidence in the officials of the board but we do not want them to say that things are all right and find they are negotiating on an unfair basis with respect to all ports. They will be judged afterwards if it is found that in any agreement there has been any question of preferential treatment.
I am happy that we are moving into the container field. The first step, of course, is the provision of container facilities, but some day we will move into the land bridge concept on which there is some disagreement, according to Mr. Cope of the transport commission. I hope Canada will move forward and take its justifiable geographic position as the centre of the giant bulk transportation system which experts feel will spread throughout the world.
The other matter I want to mention concerns an incident involving myself and two or three other members when we were returning to Ottawa from the November 11 ceremonies in the maritimes and were stuck at Dorval airport for 21 hours. This was an unbelievable occurrence. The delay was due to a freak storm. I have no quarrel with Air Canada in this regard except that I think they were too optimistic about the possibility of clearing traffic. I feel there was a mistake in judgment, but at least it was an honest one and they were probably trying to save the taxpayers' money.
As I say, we were stuck in the airport for 21 hours. We could not even get to the railway station to use the trains that were evidently still running. All this time we were wondering about the runways being cleared, and nothing was done for a great many hours. The next day, 24 hours later, just the main runway was cleared. I made inquiries about the matter. I want the minister to investigate it because Montreal is trying to be the centre of air transport in Canada and to take the overhaul base from Winnipeg. I wonder what the reason was for the runways at Dorval airport not being cleared. It was put to us unofficially that the reason was that the contract did not begin until November 15 and because it was November 12 there was no equipment at the airport.

If the minister does not believe what I say about this matter he should talk to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who was right there with us. So that hon. members will not think ministers received preferential treatment I point out that it went through my mind, as we were being herded around like peasants, that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has been forgotten in this house and in respect of matters concerning the cabinet ever since the last leadership convention, and he was just as forgotten as the rest of us on this occasion. He was forgotten at Dorval airport, because we were all herded around like sheep and had to sit in chairs all night.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I say that we have to get moving in regard to transport. I am pleased to see that the Minister without Portfolio is in the chamber. He has been following these matters. If the Minister of Transport cannot handle the matters that fall within his department and feels that housing is his main interest, I hope that changes will be made because we must have a responsible minister in charge of transportation. He must be here every day reporting on various activities with regard to transportation. Mr. Pickersgill, with all his other faults, did this. Every day he was on his feet in the house saying something, and many times not incorrectly, about transportation matters.
The minister will have the chance to reply to these questions. If he is really making the decisions I want to know what the Canadian Transport Commission is doing. The minute the shipping review was announced the other day the commission hired a group of experts in Toronto to review shipping matters. What is wrong with all the research experts in the department? We know that a former member of this house was appointed a research expert in the department at a salary of $24,000 a year. I am in favour of that. I am glad he got the job because he was a good committee chairman when in this house. I do not think he knows very much about transportation in detail but he will learn. This is all right. He has a good appreciation of over-all transportation problems. But why is it that these high-priced research experts in the department are overlooked every time the commission wants something reviewed? Why do they hire experts from outside the department? Surely there are enough experts within this department to review these questions. I would like to clarify the record at this point, Mr. Chairman. The fact that I am in
November 22, 19B8



favour of the appointment of Mr. Macaluso to this position does not mean that I agree with all the appointments made of defeated, former Liberal members.
The main consideration of the transportation committee at this time should be to finish its trip to the maritimes. This point will be developed by other members as they raise various questions. We are trying in this debate to deal with transportation matters in an orderly way. I do not think the minister appreciates what constitutes an orderly development of transportation matters, but we are trying to demonstrate it to him this afternoon.
The other day I wrote the minister a letter. I hope he received it. I received an acknowledgement of my letter. The trip to the maritimes, which was promised in the house in order to study our problems and come up with a solution, has to take place. That promise must be fulfilled. It is indelibly written and has been approved by the committee. This trip was promised to us when we agreed, though we did not vote for the transportation bill last year, thank goodness, to withhold our substantive criticism of the bill because we knew that something would be coming forward.
I believe that the trip has to be completed by March 23, 1969; otherwise the freeze will lapse and new legislation will be required. The briefs which were prepared at great expense by bodies, organizations and communities in the maritimes-I would say the cost must have been in the order of $250,000-are becoming obsolete. We may be faced with a difficult weather problem but the freeze is hovering over us, with a March deadline, and the committee trip must go forward. It may be that the minister is afraid to send the committee on this trip because the members might get stuck in a snowbank again. The minister will also recall that while we were stuck in a snowbank the government was defeated, but surely there is no worry in that regard now.
My main theme is that the department must get to work on these matters. The minister must be in the house even though the Prime Minister may not want him here. He must come into the house frequently and stand up for the department. In addition, the maritimes trip must go ahead.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, my first
remarks on the estimates of the Department
Supply-Transport
of Transport will have to do with airstrips. In Canada our airstrips are most important. We must make sure that our major air services have feeder lines from smaller centres. Moose Jaw might be taken as a good example of a community with a small airstrip. We have a private airstrip about 40 miles from the major air base at Regina and there is considerable traffic between our area and the Regina air base. Recent consultations with the airport people and Air Canada officials have confirmed the usefulness of co-operative efforts to provide means for transporting people from our area to Regina. Included in our area, of course, are Assiniboia, Weyburn and other centres in that region. I ask the minister to pay close attention to the provision of feeder lines to major airports. I believe our transport committee has some responsibility for this matter.
I now wish to say a word about Transair. One of the directors of the company is reported to have said, according to a press report:
-we had to get people who can represent us in Ottawa and elsewhere. We needed people with political know-how to tell us where to go.
He also said that most Canadian companies strive to have well connected politicians or former politicians on their boards of directors. I am sure that the other directors on the board do not appreciate that statement. I suggest there is no place for this type of obvious political patronage in our scheme of things.
Another point I wish to raise has to do with the construction of railway spur lines or branch lines. The people of Canada expend much money in various forms in building spur lines and branch lines to different localities, as was done in the case of Esterhazy. Hon. members will no doubt be aware that the International Mining Company has mined a considerable amount of potash in the area. At present 35 trucks, each holding 20 tons, deliver potash 24 hours a day to the United States town of Northgate. From there the potash is shipped via a United States railroad to Chicago or exported. The question is, why can the railroad not compete with those trucks? There are facilities at Melville for the cleaning of box cars and hopper cars. Our railroad facilities there are now rendered useless by the competition from trucks and many people in the area are losing their jobs.
Why is it that a trucking company finds it economical to transport potash from Ester-hazy when the railway does not? Is the question of management involved here? Perhaps the minister can say what is happening. I

November 22. 1968
Supply-Transport
know there have been suggestions that the Canadian National cannot compete with the trucks, but I submit that does not add up. It costs a fair amount to operate these trucks to Northgate. Roads must be cleared, repaired and maintained. I cannot see how the competitive position of the railroad has been impaired. Perhaps the minister will look into this matter. It has been suggested that some details cannot be aired in public, but I think the minister ought to investigate the entire situation.
Can the minister please tell us how deeply Canadian National Railways are involved in pipe line experimenting? It is well known that after spur lines have been built to certain areas for the benefit of certain companies in those areas the companies have experimented with pipe lines to determine whether transportation by pipe line is economically feasible. A case in point is the construction of the spur line to the Pan American Petroleum Corporation at Big Stone. The company said that Canadian National would be assured of transporting 75 per cent of the sulphur produced in that area; yet some of that sulphur has been hauled by truck. A further examination disclosed that the company is conducting research into transporting sulphur by pipe line. There is nothing wrong with transporting goods by pipe line. Nevertheless I think we ought to examine what has happened in this instance. Why should the Canadian National be asked to build a spur line and then have to compete with a pipe line? Since public moneys have been expended I think the minister ought to look into the entire matter.
I now wish to say a word about the operation of the Great Slave Lake railway. I hope the minister is not condoning what is happening there at this time since it appears that Canadian National is conducting an experiment with that railway line. It seems to me that the railway is trying to operate trains with unqualified people merely to show that it can be done. I am informed that last July there was a major accident on the line with damage amounting to thousands of dollars. I wonder who cleaned up the wreckage and who paid for the damage? It is also apparent that to date no operating order has been issued for this line. Since the railway has hauled revenue generating traffic for three years, does the minister not think it fair that there should be an operating order issued? Failure to do so in my opinion constitutes sharp practice on the part of Canadian National in this area.

I am also given to understand that a contractor is still in control of the operation of some portion of this railroad. Does the government hand this contractor money to be paid to the employees working on the railroad? If so, I think it is high time for the contractor to take his hand out of the kitty. It is time that this railroad was operated as it ought to be. We have enough qualified personnel in Canada to operate the railroad. It should not be left to an independent contractor to operate. I wish to know whether any commitments regarding the control or operation of the railroad have been made. If so, how deeply is Canadian National Railways committed in this regard?
Although many questions on this matter could be placed on the order paper I wish to ask one question in particular having to do with the operation of the Great Slave Lake railway. I wish to know what employees are now employed by the railroad both in construction work and in operating trains hauling revenue generating loads. Also, is there any effective code of uniform operating rules? If not, why not? The suggestion was made that the Board of Transport Commissioners is responsible for safety on that line. I question this statement. I believe these employees should come directly under the act as it stands today in the same way as all other employees involved in the operations of both Canadian Pacific and Canadian National.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I should like to know also exactly how far we can go in our expectations that Canadian National will assume complete responsibility at an early date. If this question were answered sincerely I believe it might also answer some of the other questions because the whole picture would fall into focus. I am wondering just how much supervision of the operation of this road is being conducted by Canadian National and also what supervision is being conducted of the contractor who is being employed in the furtherance of the construction of this line? I understand that an upgrading of the line is being carried out. I think something is lacking somewhere and it is time we knew how far the transport committee and the minister are going to go in assuming responsibility.
Another point I should like to mention relates to the unsatisfactory settlement made with some contractors employed in the construction of a portion of the Great Slave Lake railway. I am sure the minister is well aware of this problem. I will not go into all the
November 22, 1968



details at this time, but I suggest that many contractors have tried unsuccessfully to have a settlement made of their outstanding claims against the Canadian National or the major contractor who was in charge of the construction of this line. We feel it is important that these contractors be given an answer forthwith. I am quite sure the construction of this line was embarked upon in the interests of this area. I am quite sure also that the many contractors involved are entitled to an answer to their inquiries as to why they have not been paid. Why has there not been a satisfactory arrangement made for the disposition of their outstanding claims? I am sure the minister could give me an answer that would help in this regard.
I was pleased to hear the minister refer to the amount of money expended from the grade crossing fund. I am sure he appreciates the fact that we can spend many thousands of dollars in the elimination of hazardous conditions at railway crossings. I am sure he appreciates also that some of these types of protection do not go far enough. I am pleased to learn that the National Research Council has done a considerable amount of work in this regard. I am pleased to learn too that other means of protection are being offered. I feel it is time the transport committee looked at alternative methods of protection against the hazards to highway traffic which exist at railway crossings. Many other methods of protection have to be examined, as a result of increasing highway traffic, in addition to the ordinary bells, gates, lights and so on. Many hazardous conditions exist today which result from the types of commodities being carried now by trucks. Therefore we can no longer allow this situation to continue. I am pleased to note that definite improvements are being considered.
There is one other point upon which I should like the minister to comment briefly when he answers. Just what control do we have over the passenger operations of the Canadian Pacific? I understand that a deliberate attempt has been made to downgrade the Canadian by reducing the number of cars on that train to as low as ten. Every member of this house appreciates how difficult it is to obtain space on that train. It is difficult to obtain space on Canadian National trains, but I must commend the Canadian National for its progressive attitude toward passenger traffic. I should like to know whether the Canadian Pacific would have to go before the
Supply-Transport
transport commission before it could downgrade the Canadian further by removing the sleeping car facilities. The rumours are that the Canadian Pacific intends to put on a day-liner from Winnipeg to Calgary. If this is so, I should like to know in order that these communities can be notified. I am sure everyone here realizes that this is something that should not and absolutely cannot be allowed.
I should like now to deal with the research program. Many questions have been asked about this program and the new director of the research division of the Canadian Transport Commission. Just what qualifications did that individual have when he applied for the job? I understand that when the requirements for this position were published they were quite restrictive. Did the director actually meet every one of those requirements?
I should like to know also what are the terms of reference of this research division. If this would involve a lengthy answer, perhaps the minister could give it in writing later. It seems to me that we go along consistently adding more research departments but we do not know what type of research they are doing. I am sure that if members were more fully aware of the research that was being conducted they could appreciate the various phases of research.
I should like to refer again to the National Research Council which I feel is doing an excellent job. The council issues an excellent report which enables us to appreciate the work being done. I am not too sure that we fully appreciate the research program that is being undertaken. If it means, in effect, that we are hiring a large group of people just for the purpose of eliminating positions farther down the line, then we might have to consider that fact. I realize that management has to do this sort of thing, but I would question just what the terms of reference of this research branch are and whether it should be given encouragement at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair until 2.30 p.m.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, another point I wish to bring up concerns the existing situation at Roberts Bank. The transportation committee has discussed this situation but it appears that many factors are shrouded in secre-

November 22, 1968
Supply-Transport
cy and the committee was unable to obtain clearcut answers to some of its questions. It is absolutely imperative that the minister and the government let the people know what is happening in this regard.
In this connection, I should like to pose one or two questions that might help to clear up the situation. First of all, who is going to control the rail line between Crows Nest and Roberts Bank? Who will set the freight rates over this stretch of line? Who is going to set the charges for transporting coal over the new rail line to Roberts Bank? By how much will these charges add to the cost of a ton of coal?
Another facet of the Roberts Bank situation concerns a matter that has been raised in the house, namely, the question of jurisdiction over the facilities in the area. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has tried unsuccessfully to find out what action the government intends to take with regard to the problem of constitutional jurisdiction. The hon. member for Kootenay West has also been attempting to get answers as to the jurisdictional problems that are involved in connection with the rail route to Roberts Bank. It would be appreciated if the minister would clear up any misunderstanding that may exist and put the record straight on this question.
I believe it is most important to the people most concerned that they be consulted about the location of the rail route in that area. I am referring to the lower mainland regional planning board. The courtesy should at least have been extended to them of prior consultation as to the location of the rail line, and the railroads concerned should have seen fit to contact the board about this matter. There have been too many innuendoes and arguments made about whether jurisdiction in this area lies with the provincial or the federal government. I am sure the minister recognizes that it is absolutely imperative for the National Harbours Board to have control and administration of ports. There would be a real hodge-podge if we were to allow a province to control one port and the federal government to control another. There would be a continual breakdown of relations.
There is another aspect I should like to refer to. In my opinion it is quite impossible for the present minister to handle the two portfolios of housing and transportation. I cannot see any relation between building a home and providing facilities therefor and constructing railroads to transport people. I
[Mr. Skoberg.l
hope that the Prime Minister will see fit to divide the functions of the minister because it is apparent to me that his present burdensome task is too much for one man to handle effectively.
I concur completely with some of the statements made by the previous hon. member in regard to the Canadian Transport Commission. I understand that the president of the C.T.C. is being referred to as the czar of transportation in Canada. I would hate to see "czar" change into "scar". It appears to me that too much authority is invested in one department for this state of affairs to continue any longer. The minister must be given time to take a really close look at the whole transportation field.
Another point I want to raise concerns the port of Churchill. I am sure the minister will give us some insight as to any future plans for this port to increase the volume of imports and exports. In my opinion it is fairly well substantiated that savings can be effected by using this port. For example, the shipping season could be extended beyond the present limit. We are aware of the fact that the marine insurance season is now the deciding factor, but I believe that in light of the facts the federal government should lead the way in suggesting that the marine insurance season be extended so that additional time could be made available to export wheat. With additional exports of potash, oil and so on such an extension would be very beneficial.
The first Canadian urban transportation conference is going to be held in Toronto from February 9 to 12. I would like to congratulate the minister on what he has done to assist this conference. I would also congratulate the federation of mayors and municipalities for arranging the conference. I ask the minister to consider seriously sending a goodly delegation from the present transportation committee to the conference in order that the delegation may learn at first hand what is happening in this field today. They have published a pamphlet headed "Opportunity Or Chaos", which I am sure the minister realizes is actually the position in which the entire field of transportation finds itself today. I ask the minister to make sure that as many members as possible attend the conference so that they can take an intelligent look at the picture in all its aspects.

As far as the Air Canada overhaul base at Winnipeg is concerned, it has been clearly established that the government would save millions of dollars in having its repairs made at Montreal rather than in Winnipeg. I should like to talk this afternoon about the proposed expansion of the international airport at Malton which was announced in August by the Minister of Transport. He stated this was to be a two-phase operation and that the first phase would carry us to approximately 1973 and would involve the expansion of passenger handling facilities on the ground and perhaps some modification of runways, but there would be no major changes as far as land use or runways were concerned. He was careful to point out at the time of his announcement that this was no more than a proposed expansion and that the closely associated communities would be invited to discuss compatible land use with the federal government.
At the same time the minister also pointed out that it was important to work out arrangements with the provinces in respect of handling of traffic and access. He reaffirmed this in the house last week and I think again this week. The implicit undertaking is, of course, that unless satisfactory arrangements can be worked out the proposals will not go forward in the form first suggested.
I was very happy, as I know all members from the Toronto region and indeed of this house were, to hear the emphasis the minister placed on the importance of the quality of life in reaching a decision on whether or not the proposed expansion would go forward in the form first presented. The question I think we

have to concern ourselves with is, what does the proposed expansion of Malton airport mean to the quality of life of those who live in Etobicoke, Mississagua and north?
The essential statistics at the present time indicate that at Malton slightly more than four million passengers a year are moved, that it is expected passenger traffic will build to a little more than double that by 1973, and that in the order of about nineteen million will be moved by 1985. The statistics also indicate that if this expansion goes forward the airport will handle close to 19 million people per year. There will also be a more than corresponding increase in freight handling.
We must concern ourselves with the type of aircraft that will be involved in this type of utilization as a result of the change from the jet as we know it today to the jumbo jet and to the supersonic jet with engines of greater power and, one can only assume at this stage, engines which will make more noise. Noise is the essential factor as far as the quality of life is concerned for those most directly associated with these airports.
Let me refer to the measurement most frequently used, being 100 decibels. This is considered to be above the level at which people can live with any degree of comfort; yet thousands are now being exposed to a level of this magnitude on a daily basis. With the proposed expansion to its ultimate form the figures I have-they are no more than estimates at the present time but reliable ones- indicate that about 160,000 people would be exposed to this noise level on a regular basis.
In assessing these problems in regard to Malton airport and what sort of expansion, if any, should take place, one has to recognize that at the start Malton represents a major investment estimated at $70 million with probably a replacement value very much greater than that. This is an investment which all the people of Canada have made. It is an investment by the community at large. One has to recognize the economic arguments in favour of employment, the creation of new service industries and growth. One must also recognize the needs of the traveller, whether for business purposes or for pleasure. One must recognize the claims of the pilots in respect of safety for those who would land these planes at this airport. One has also to recognize the carriers, those who are providing the aircraft.

The form of transport which I really think should be investigated is the pipe line system. As people, we do not like to think of ourselves being propelled through a pipe line. Most of us are familiar with the apparatus used in some stores by means of which money and messages are sped through tubes by use of a vacuum. This principle can be applied on a much larger scale to carry cargo and human beings. Right-of-way problems would be greatly reduced because, of course, a tube can be buried underground. Here again, containers could be specially designed, and aircraft could be built to accommodate these containers. We might indeed reach a stage at which every passenger had his own little container; we would be loaded into the tube with our luggage and remain there until reaching our destination.
