As I understand the hon. minister he is saying that it is a great mistake, in respect of the national economy, to take a laissez-faire attitude and not take an interest in the phenomenon whereby more and more industry and more and more technical capability becomes crammed into one or two metropolitan complexes, while the rest of the country remains underdeveloped and some areas which have been slow developing slide back. In connection with the great metropolitan complex of Montreal I should like to say it is my understanding that because of the tremendous increase in air traffic in the next few years it will be necessary to spend many millions of dollars to extend the air terminal facilities at Montreal. No one is complaining about that. This is an obvious necessity and one which will be taken care of by any government at the federal level. In addition to that, however, it is my understanding that not only will millions of dollars be spent on expanding the air terminal facilities but also that it will be necessary for Air Canada to spend millions of dollars in increasing its jet aircraft hangar facilities. This is something that was not taken into account at the time when one or two inquiry commissions made their inquiry and report on the problem of the location of the Air Canada base.
I should like the Minister of Transport to indicate clearly whether or not it is a fact that in the next decade there will be a major capital expenditure for increased air terminal facilities at Montreal. In addition, would the minister indicate clearly whether it is in the plans of Air Canada to spend a major amount
November 22, 1968

of money in capital construction costs to increase the size of the jet engine overhaul and hangar facilities at Montreal. If that should be true, then it does in a substantial way impinge upon the decision as to whether or not there is a purely economic overwhelming case that this overhaul base should be transferred from Winnipeg to Montreal.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There is much more I should like to say in this connection, but since I made some reference to the subject not long ago I shall desist from saying anything more at this time. It is difficult for me to understand the hon. member for Temiscamingue-not my colleague, but the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste- who said, and I believe I understood him correctly, that we must consider the problem of the location of the Air Canada base "stric-tement du point de vue economique": that is, strictly from an economic point of view. I was surprised to hear the hon. member say that, because he knows full well that other considerations are involved. He has had to fight hard during the past five years for the establishment of a policy in our crown corporations and the C.N.R., which should be used as an instrument reflecting the bilingual character of this country. You cannot look at these operations all the time strictly from the point of view of economics. If that were so, how could one hope to persuade these crown corporations that they should, even at extra expense, undertake to provide services in a bilingual manner in order to meet the needs of Canadians, regardless of whether they are French or English speaking? The hon. member for Temiscamingue was not taking the position that the operations of our crown corporations must be looked at only from an economic point of view, because at times there are other factors which become overriding.
In connection with the Air Canada base at Winnipeg and whether it should be removed completely and added to the already large operation at Montreal, this does not involve just a matter of the internal operation of that crown corporation but also the question as to the regional needs in different parts of the country. We must consider whether we should put our eggs in one basket and follow the trend of some of the so-called banana republics, where everything is crammed into one or two large metropolitan cities and the rest of the country remains in extreme poverty and squalor with very little opportunity. This is what is involved, not just the internal
Supply-Transport
economic operations of crown corporations and balance sheets.
At this time I wish to refer to a subject which has been touched upon by two previous speakers on the other side of the house, the hon. members for Etobicoke and York North. They ventured to suggest that within the Department of Transport a greater effort should be made, either under the aegis of the D.O.T. or a separate body, to perform a greater amount of research in the field of transportation, its economics, the implications of new modes of transportation and public health and safety. I am in complete agreement. Neither of those gentlemen referred to research into the effects of sound, but mentioned only research in respect of noise, as they put it. They mentioned noise in relation to public health and safety, or the dangers involved.
It is my feeling that this idea should be extended to encompass research into the effects of sound, not just noise, which implies sound at the upper decibel range. We should also consider sound which is imperceptive to the human ear; the sounds of high frequencies, supersonics and so on. It is my conviction, having been interested for several months in this matter, that the Department of Transport, although it performs the function of licensing of equipment and operators, does not really know what the safe permissive standard of radiant energy emission is. I would not say that if I did not feel convinced that this is so. There are a number of officials in the Department of Transport licensing branch whose function it is to check all applications for telecommunications equipment operations. Presumably they check to make sure that the power output is within a frequency range, and issue a license on the assumption that the equipment will operate within that acceptable range and that the power output will not be such as to pose a threat to public health and safety.
Much more research has been done in the United States in this regard than here in Canada. Many millions of dollars have been spent in this area and the people there are much more uncertain and uneasy about their standards of safety than we are in Canada. This is a very puzzling situation. If one asks the Department of Transport here whether it is satisfied that a microwave tower emitting energy at the rate of about 5 watts, at a frequency range of 6,000 megacycles, is safe, he is told it comes within the standards which have been accepted for a number of years

November 22, 1968
Supply-Transport
and that there cannot be any possibility of danger.
I have found from reading through some of the records of the hearings by the United States senate commerce committee, on this topic of radiation control for health safety, that the top experts in the United States agree almost unanimously, or certainly by an overwhelming majority, that the standards maintained there during the past decade are seriously out of date. They suggest they are crude, require refinement and that a better assessment of standards should be made. The standards upon which we issue licences do not take into account the possible non-thermal effect of radiant energy over long periods of time on human tissue, and forms of biological plant and animal life.
What are we doing in this country to deal with this problem or potential hazard? It is becoming more important with each passing year that something be done, because there is an increasing use of this kind of equipment. There is greater use by military authorities and the telecommunications industry. Beginning about two years ago there has been a steady increase in the use of this type of equipment in kitchens. Many ovens are equipped to use microwave radiant energy to cook foods.
The examples I have given represent only a small part of this phenomenon, which is growing with the state of knowledge in this area. I say without apology or wish to hurt anyone's feelings that our research and understanding in this regard is extremely inadequate. Our Department of Agriculture is conducting some research in this field. It has granted $3,000 to the University of Manitoba for research into the potential hazards of the thermal effect of microwave radiation and microwave energy. I suggest this is nonsense. Any research worthy of the name in this field must engage itself over a long period of time in field conditions, and not just laboratory conditions. It must concern itself with research into possible non-thermal effects of microwave and electrical frequency radiation. I am not speaking futuristically when I say there is an urgent need in this respect. The need is now. Since the Department of Transport issues licences for the operation of this equipment, it must undertake the research and not leave it to the Department of Agriculture. The Department of National Health and Welfare is not carrying out this research either. There does not seem to be any liaison between the departments that

might be concerned, and to the extent that there is research it is inadequate not only in terms of dollars and cents but in the terms of reference. All in all, it is a pretty sad situation.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the suggestion of the hon. member for York North and others for more research by the D.O.T. is accepted. I hope this research will be undertaken in a more comprehensive way, rather than confining it to noise. I hope the research will direct itself to the possible harmful effects of sound on all ranges, and radiation energy.
I would like to put on the record excerpts from the hearings held before a United States Congress committee, but because of the time factor and the fact that other hon. members wish to speak on these estimates I will deny myself that temptation. I feel tempted, however, to send to the Minister of Transport not just a few excerpts but all three volumes of the hearings, so that he will not treat this matter cavalierly and with indifference.
Another matter I should like to mention is the attitude of the Department of Transport with respect to regional air carriers. I know that the D.O.T. is preoccupied with our large-scale rail and air operations, but in Canada there are air lines of small and intermediate size that are of significant importance to the economies of their areas. I find, just as the hon. member for Churchill has been pointing out in the last few days, that the Department of Transport is not very much concerned with the operating difficulties which some of our regional air lines have to face.
Let us take, for example, the Winnipeg international airport complex. The regional air carriers-and there are a number of them often find it difficult to get enough hangar space, area space, in order to service, maintain and overhaul their aircraft. They find it difficult, therefore, to always meet their licence requirements in terms of frequency of service, and the like, and this becomes an increasing problem to them. This is a pity indeed, because for the northern areas of every province, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and others-in fact, from sea to sea-the importance of the smaller carriers cannot be overestimated. To the extent that the Department of Transport is unco-operative in assisting these air carriers to maintain their operations, the department is doing a disservice to the economic development and servicing of the north country.
November 22, 1968

A few days ago, in a rather informal way and at rather short notice someone in the Department of Transport-I suspect it was the minister or the minister without portfolio from Winnipeg, or both of them-ordered the convening of a meeting at Winnipeg to which were invited the regional, smaller air carriers. This meeting was convened because there has been a persistent problem over the last few years for these air line managers and operators to obtain co-operation from the Department of Transport with regard to getting hangar space.
I want to know how much longer this situation will persist. The Department of National Defence has a few air force hangars there. The rumour is that for long periods of time these hangars are under-utilized and could be made available on a rental basis to some of the smaller air line operators. This has not been done. I think the Department of Transport could give some help in this regard. The leasing policy of the department is not any help. As I understand the situation at the airport sites, they insist upon only short term leases and expect the smaller air lines to build permanent facilities. There is a need for conciliation to solve this problem.
I think it would be just as well, Mr. Chairman, if I resumed my place. I have drawn to the attention of the minister and his associate three problems which I consider to be important at the present time. One is the question of the proposed move of the overhaul base from Winnipeg; the second is the lack of enthusiasm by the Department of Transport with regard to accommodating the needs of regional air carriers and smaller air line operators in different parts of the country, with particular reference to Winnipeg; and the third is the need for vastly expanded research by the D.O.T. in the area of the hazard and threat to public health and safety of various forms of microwave energy, which is the form of energy used in telecommunications and which the D.O.T. licenses.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to answer as many questions as possible in the few minutes remaining this afternoon. May I begin by answering some of the questions raised by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster. With regard to the Robinson report which was received in October, 1967, I can say that the department has been actively engaged in the evaluation and implementation of the recommendations. The recommendations covered a broad range of activities-
Supply-Transport
organization, recruitment, training, personnel matters and operational equipment.
Many of the recommendations respecting terms and conditions of employment are subject to the collective bargaining process. In this regard the Canadian air traffic controllers and the employer completed negotiation of their first collective agreement in August of this year. The tremendous growth in aviation has required that there be continuing improvement and adjustment in the air traffic control services-recruitment, staffing, training, equipment, etc.-on a programmed basis to keep pace with the requirements and maintain the department's standard of safety, which is second to none in any country. The hon. member also raised the question of general assistance to the Atlantic area, maritimes freight rates assistance, less-than-carload lot rates, and so on.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I will not take much time to deal with the matter at the moment. I shall merely assure my hon. friend that we are undertaking a very active study. A day or two ago I had a chance to speak to one of the people directly involved in the task force which was established by the Atlantic premiers. He has indicated they are well advanced with their thinking and we should have a report from them in a few weeks. In the meantime the studies which have been done by the Canadian Transport Commission have been going forward in parallel, so that we may look at them both concurrently. Very early in the new year we hope to give these our undivided attention in the hope that we can come to some conclusion designed to provide the best value with regard to transportation facilities for the people of the Atlantic region.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
May I interrupt the minister, Mr. Chairman. Will he undertake, say in the next two weeks at some appropriate time, to say something about the matter of the expiry of the freeze on certain types of rates. I ask that, since it looks as if we shall have no new legislation before March. That is our insurmountable problem. I assume the minister agrees that the freeze will cause trouble. I understand the governor in council might be able to deal with it; but since this matter is fairly important and looms large I should appreciate an assurance from the minister with regard to the expiry of the freeze on rates. That might be enough for the time being.

November 22, 1968
Supply-Transport

I do not think I can give that commitment, Mr. Chairman, because it is related to all the other aspects of Atlantic transportation. I would not want to comment on one aspect, when that might be out of context with other aspects.
With regard to the other reports referred to by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster that come within the jurisdiction of the department, I can assure the committee that work is proceeding as quickly and as effectively as possible.
With regard to revising the Canada Shipping Act, an outside consultant has been engaged to take an independent view of the research work done by our own experts, as well as to recommend a form that new legislation ought to take.
With regard to the report of the royal commission on pilotage, the government has received the first part of the five part report and a team of departmental officials has been established to prepare the groundwork for policy decisions by the government, in addition to those already known to my hon. friend.
The hon. member also wanted to know what happened at Dorval on November 11. Perhaps the hon. member's knowledge is more extensive than mine. In any event, the department has sufficient equipment to keep the airport open and, as a matter of fact, runways were never closed at any time during the storm in question. The aircraft parking apron was, however, in a bad condition, because of inability to move snow off the apron. Trucking of snow off the airport was carried out by contract; the airport was not equipped with trucks for this purpose. The contractor was advised that his services would be required by a stated time but his trucks were unable to reach the airport, due to the blockage of roads leading to the airport. Vehicular traffic was completely disrupted due to stalled cars, etc., and some of the airport staff who left work at 4 p.m. did not reach their homes until midnight. Operations at the airport were suspended for ten hours due to a combination of blockage of road traffic to the airport, conditions of the parking apron and visibility. The latter factor was instrumental in many airlines suspending their operations. The storm in question was the worst in years in the Montreal area from the point of view of snowfall. I assure my hon. friend that I will speak to the personnel of our meteorological branch and ask them to see that this does not happen again.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: May I interject, Mr. Chairman that we, who were on the way to the House of Commons in Ottawa, were most upset because we could not find the V.I.P. room until five o'clock in the morning.
It must not happen again.
Is that the washroom?

I think I had better not comment further on that interjection. The hon. member for Moose Jaw inquired about extending the season at the port of Churchill. We have a study nearing completion that deals with the extension of the shipping season. This is being carried out, with some degree of co-operation, with the Manitoba royal commission investigating the future of northern Manitoba. It is expected that a preliminary finding will be available in published form within three or four months. I can also assure my hon. friend that at the proposed first urban conference on transportation, members of this house will be represented. I hope they will include some members of our transport committee.
The hon. member for Temiscamingue asked for consideration with respect to the continuation of trains 83 and 84. I am sure he will appreciate that this is a matter for the Canadian Transport Commission and that representations should be made to the railway committee of that commission when public hearings are held. I noted, however, a slight degree of inconsistency in the hon. member's remarks. Although he insisted that the decision respecting the Winnipeg air base should be made strictly on economic grounds, he said that these trains ought to be kept in service notwithstanding-and I took this admission from his remarks-that they are not economical. This lack of consistency appears from time to time in public life and must be taken into account when future plans are being made.
That is a good sentence.

It is one I copied from a former holder of the office now occupied by the hon. gentleman.
The hon. member for Etobicoke made an excellent representation on behalf of the residents of his riding advising against the major expansion at Toronto international airport. He raised a number of problems which are indeed relevant. All I can say at this time is that they were also raised by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants and all those
November 22, 19G8

factors that have been raised will be taken into consideration before a final decision is made. I think that has been understood from the beginning. There are many factors in favour of the major expansion, although there are good reasons to know that would disturb quite a number of people. I can only assure my hon. friends that all points of view will be listened to and considered before we make a final decision.
The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate asked a number of questions. I shall only deal with one of them as my time has almost expired. He mentioned the Carmanville-Fogo subsidy. I can only say that this is administered by the water transport committee. Perhaps the hon. member could pass his question to the Canadian Transport Commission and have it dealt with before the committee of that commission. In addition he asked about the possibility of extending the runway at Gander. In that regard I have a letter which I will send him in answer to an earlier inquiry. It states, in effect, that the department will expand these runways when there is a demand for this from the users. At present we have not been requested, either by international or domestic users of this airport, to expand the runway facilities there. These questions are constantly under review and if it is decided that an additional runway is required in order to facilitate the landings of aircraft, that of course will be taken into consideration by the department.
The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants raised a question similar to the one raised by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster with respect to maritime transportation generally. I can also assure him that this matter will come under very active consideration in the weeks ahead and I hope it will not be too long before a report on the matter is presented.
He also asked for consideration to be given to providing flights from Halifax to places like Ottawa. I expect he realizes that this will come about when traffic is sufficient to support that kind of service. A number of new services have been inaugurated; for example, there is a flight now from Winnipeg to Ottawa. Without doubt a great many more services will come into being in the months and years ahead as additional traffic is generated.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The hon. member for York North made a very interesting speech in which he proposed
Supply-Transport
a far out, but perhaps not that far out, alternative to the expansion of Toronto international airport. In doing so he also raised a number of interesting ideas and suggestions in respect of urban development in the broader sense, and better value in housing. I was therefore listening in both capacities and trying to put the whole scheme together in my mind. I can only thank him for at least stretching our minds a little by giving us these ideas to consider.
The hon. member for Selkirk mentioned his concern about the five watt microwave transmitter of 6,000 megacycles. I should like to remind him, not as an indication of my lack of concern, that during the war radar was operated on the order of one million watts without any harmful effects being observed. At the same time I can assure my hon. friend we are interested and concerned in adding to the total bank of scientific knowledge relating to modern technological developments. I am sure there is a lot we do not know as yet. I am sure, too, that the hon. member knows that the sun radiates energy not far from this section of the spectrum. This, too, has effects on the human body which are not fully appreciated.
Will the minister permit a question?

I think perhaps the next time around, because there is one more answer I should like to give and I have already transgressed on the good nature of the house to the extent of an extra five minutes.
In so far as the Winnipeg airport is concerned, I should like to advise that recently there were negotiations between my department and the Department of National Defence as a result of which the Department of National Defence agreed to make available to us half of hangar No. 4, that is on the east side. This space will be available immediately and will partially accommodate the traffic there. We have also made an arrangement for a parcel of land adjacent to hangar No. 4. Next summer we will commence construction of additional facilities on that parcel. Furthermore, the consultant's long range study that the government requested has been considered by our department. This is the subject of further negotiations which are presently taking place with the Department of National Defence and will enable us to provide additional facilities. I think it will not be too long before we will be able to provide adequate facilities for commercial users at Winnipeg.

Supply-Transport
Finally, Mr. Chairman, may I thank all hon. gentlemen who have participated in the debate this afternoon. I think they have been most constructive in their interventions and I hope that if there are any questions remaining we can deal with them at a future date, or on orders of the day.

I should point out, of course, as is indicated in the motion, that this day comes off the very limited number of days available to the house for supply. in addition to being concerned with their ordinary work over a full session, are confronted by an additional work load.

subtopic: CONDITIONAL ADMISSION OF MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext:
Thank you. I was motivated to introduce this bill by the troubles and appeals of a number of people in my area of British Columbia who are parents of mentally retarded children and members of the local Mental Retardation Society. Their complaint, which they still make today, Mr. Speaker, is that when they and their families visit across the border in Washington, Oregon and other states with their children who are mentally retarded, they run into a good deal of trouble and delay. As we can understand, people with mentally retarded children have so many troubles in the ordinary course of events that they naturally wish if possible to avoid additional friction when visiting relations or friends in another part of this continent. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I am trying to put forward in legislative form the suggestion that families who come from the United States to visit Canada and who similarly have mentally retarded members should not run into similar difficulty in our border restrictions.
The hope of the families on behalf of whom I speak was, and still is, that if Canada would reform and update our border crossing regulations in this respect it might well be that this would encourage the making of a mutual arrangement with our neighbours to the south, the United States, in regard to their regulations. The explanatory note to Bill No. C-10 which I have put forward reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to provide that a person afflicted with mental retardation may be

Immigration Act Amendment admitted to Canada under the Immigration Act if he is not likely to become a public charge.
In other words-the absolute prohibition against such a person is relaxed to the degree applicable to persons who are "dumb, blind, or otherwise physically defective".
The phrase which I have used dumb, blind, or otherwise physically defective" appears in section 5 of our present Immigration Act, which deals with prohibited classes. Under existing laws these persons may be admitted to Canada if they have sufficient means of support, if they are not likely to become public charges, or are members of a family accompaying them or already in Canada and the family gives satisfactory security against such immigrants becoming public charges.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house would provide similar safeguards and privileges for members of families who are mentally retarded to come into this country. The effect of the bill would be to eliminate the additional trouble caused those families with mentally retarded members when crossing the United States border into Canada. Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, the country to our south, the United States, would respond by passing similar legislation.
The intent of the bill was to ease, if this is possible, entry from the United States to Canada of families with mentally retarded members, in the hope, as I say, of reciprocal legislation. This restriction was to be lifted for visits only. However, as drafted the bill would also provide for the visit or permanent entry into Canada of such persons, with the safeguards that I have enumerated.
There are, of course, provisions in the United States in the form of waivers to help in this sort of situation. I believe these waivers are attached to the entry visa and provide a way around the prohibition that exists in their immigration legislation in regard to mentally retarded people. I am also informed that for our part Canada has a similar type of waiver which can be applied for in order to permit the entry of such persons.
However, in both countries the actual immigration legislation does not in itself provide for what, to me at least, seems a common sense, humanitarian thing, namely the entry without special application of people who conform to the provisions in the act regarding persons who are dumb, blind or otherwise physically defective.
I have in front of me the current issue, fall 1968, of the publication "Mental Retardation". The general question that my bill concerns 

itself with-that is, the passage across the international border of the type of person I have described in the bill-is very well dealt with, to the extent of several pages. A chapter dealing with the retarded and border crossing regulations is included in the pamphlet for the information and help of people concerned, namely those families with mentally retarded members who wish to make visits to or take up permanent residence in the United States or Canada, as the case may be. There are certain regulations in both countries with which these people must concur, and the chapter describes in detail over the course of several pages the different steps that should be taken to surmount the prohibition that exists in the legislation. It ends by saying:
It is perhaps unnecessary to point out how archaic these provisions in the Immigration Act are. Changes should be made to reflect more adequately the social and economic realities of present day life.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The same idea as is expressed in the publication from which I have quoted, and in my own bill, was also put forward by the former minister of citizenship and immigration, now the minister responsible for forestry and rural development (Mr. Marchand). In 1966 a white paper was issued under the name of that hon. gentleman in which the following is stated in section 58 under the heading Immigration Policy:
Scientific knowledge and medical skill have reduced substantially the element of risk once inherent in certain illnesses. The present grounds for prohibition do not altogether reflect this advance. Nor are they altogether in line with modem medical and sociological concepts, particularly in respect of mental illness and epilepsy. Persons actually insane or suffering from contagious or infectious diseases ought not to be admitted as immigrants or non-immigrants, unless they are coming to Canada by previous arrangement and under proper safeguards to take treatment. However, an illness that has been cured or brought under control to the point where no danger to public health or safety exists, should not be a bar to either temporary or permanent admission.
Nor should mental or physical defectives be excluded for that reason alone, but only if they represent a danger to society or are not assured of private care.
With this I fully agree, and I urge the house to give at least approval in principle this evening to the subject matter of the proposed bill so that it may be proceeded with at committee level.

subtopic: CONDITIONAL ADMISSION OF MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext:
The
purpose of this bill, as outlined by the hon.
November 22, 1968

member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) is to provide that a person afflicted with mental retardation may be admitted to Canada under the Immigration Act, if he is not likely to become a public charge. In other words, the prohibition against the admission to Canada as a landed immigrant of such person would be removed.
I wish to commend the hon. member for his humanitarian attitude, because I have also had the privilege of introducing bills of similar intent which had the effect of proposing amendments to the Immigration Act. In my case, the proposed amendments were designed to give permanent status to immigrants who had suffered mental disorders, who had been admitted to a mental institution after their admission to Canada as landed immigrants, and who had apparently been cured. I am referring to the introduction of Bill C-30. I was very fortunate in that this bill was accepted by the government, and that on March 22 of this year the amendment which I had proposed became law.
As a former parliamentary secretary to two ministers of citizenship and immigration, I am naturally in sympathy with the objective which the bill under discussion would achieve, if approved by parliament, and I welcome the opportunity to make a few observations about it. First of all, I would agree that a person afflicted with mental retardation should not always be regarded as hopeless. Recent advances in medical knowledge and techniques may well, in some cases, have the effect of alleviating the affliction. From a report on mental retardation by the executive director of the National Association for Retarded Children, I wish to quote the following:
Historically, mental retardation has been viewed for the most part as a static, unchanging, incurable condition. Although there were some brilliant thinkers and gifted practitioners who envisioned the potentials of training and treatment for the retarded, the idea "Once retarded always retarded" led over the years to the general practice of providing humane treatment with little hope that the afflicted individuals could ever participate in the competitive world of employment and civic responsibility.
Indeed, the concept had so strongly crystallized that, in 1916, Terman described the mentally retarded as follows-"They will make a little progress in a well-managed special class, but with the approach of adolescence, at latest, the state should take them into custodial care for its own protection." Terman held that mental retardation was inherited-that mental deficiency and moral deficiency were synonymous, that mental growth stopped in adolescence, and that since intelligence was a general problem-solving behaviour then if one was retarded at all one was
Immigration Act Amendment
retarded in each specific area of human functioning. With this type of concept, it is small wonder that little effort was made to try and improve the performance of the mentally retarded.
Several years ago, as a matter of fact, scientists were working to lay the foundation for a revolution in the physical sciences, one which has changed our lives and is changing them every day. Our present world has been transformed by the great scientific revolution of the last quarter of a century, from television to the space rocket. Science has created a new world with new problems, dangers and challenges. A number of Nobel prize winners have devoted themselves to the subject of mental retardation. For example, in 1958 a man by the name of Lederberg shared the Nobel prize for uncovering some of the basic mechanisms underlying heredity and worked in the Kennedy laboratories devoted to mental retardation. A Dr. Lejeune from France won the Kennedy award by proving that certain characteristics in the cells of the human body offer hope of controlling some forms of mental retardation. Another scientist by the name of Donald Glaser, winner of a Nobel prize in physics, was so interested in mental retardation that he switched his field of interest to microbiology, feeling that in this field lay the challenge of the future. The work of these scientists who are seeking an understanding of the human mind and body, together with the processes of fundamental life, will have consequences for the surprisingly vast number of the mentally retarded in Canada as well as for the millions elsewhere in the world.
It has been reliably reported that nearly half a million Canadians suffer the handicap of mental retardation in one degree or another. In other words, it is estimated that about 3 per cent of Canadians are to some extent retarded. Only four other disabling conditions, mental illness, cardiac disease, arthritis and cancer have a higher prevalence, and these tend to come later in life, whereas mental retardation comes early.
Mental retardation ranks as a major national health, social and economic problem. It afflicts twice as many individuals as blindness, polio, cerebral palsy and rheumatic heart disease combined. Mental retardation does not respect station in life, or geography. It may afflict the children of the rich, or of the poor, in any part of the country.
Great strides have been made in learning new ways to educate and rehabilitate those, who a few years ago, had no hope. The Canadian Association for Retarded Children, the
November 22, 1968

Immigration Act Amendment Canadian Mental Health Association, and others, have made outstanding efforts to help the mentally retarded. But surveys made by the Canadian Association for Retarded Children, its member associations and other organizations, reveal a serious shortage of facilities for mentally retarded children and adults alike.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The great hope of these handicapped persons lies in the implementation of the many new concepts developed in treatment, training, vocational guidance and permanent care, which will bring about a greater integration of the mentally handicapped into the community, and more humane treatment for those whose disabilities are so severe as to require constant supervision.
I have no hesitation in saying that in my view the problem of mental retardation has been neglected, and only in recent years have we become conscious of the need to do something about it. In order successfully to meet the problem more co-ordinated efforts should be made on the part of the municipalities, the provinces, and the federal government.
In 1964 there was the first Canadian federal-provincial conference on mental retardation. The conference was conceived as a timely and essential step in seeking to improve, extend and achieve greater co-ordination of health, welfare, education and vocational services for mentally retarded children and adults.
Following the conference a steering committee met in Ottawa in February 1965, to review the work of the conference. The committee felt that it was the federal government's responsibility to provide leadership by working with the provincial authorities and voluntary health and welfare groups. It felt that attention should be given to mental retardation in mental health research, child and maternal health research, and related research programs. It believed that the conference itself had indicated that there were many avenues to improve services and better co-ordination of agencies and facilities, and that to pursue these required only a spirit of conscious concern on the part of all responsible persons. The committee also felt that the conference, in heightening this sense of conscious concern, had accomplished its major purpose.
What we have been able in past to accomplish for the mentally retarded in Canada is


only a beginning when related to the great accomplishments that we can attain in the years ahead. I suggest that we should accept a more responsible role in the field of mental retardation, as our knowledge expands in this great field of public welfare which offers avenues of hope undreamed of in the past.
In my opinion the bill in question could well be broader, affecting not only paragraph (s) of section 5 of the Immigration Act, but it might well have also dealt with section 5(a) (iv) which refers to those afflicted with epilepsy. This is also an affliction that has responded to new medical knowledge and techniques.
However, I must point out that the bill which I have referred to as Bill C-30 dealt with an amendment to give permanent status under the Immigration Act to immigrants who have suffered from a mental disorder, but who apparently have been cured. The minister realized that when the Immigration Act was framed insanity was regarded as an incurable illness, and saw the merit of the need for a change in the act. We are all grateful to the former minister of manpower and immigration for his foresight and humane understanding, from which many immigrants are enjoying the benefits in the change of the legislation, restoring to them the dignity and the right to apply for Canadian citizenship which was denied to them under an unfair section in the Immigration Act.
Whether paragraph (s) of section 5 of the Immigration Act, which this bill is trying to change, is unfair, has to be examined in the light of circumstances surrounding individual cases. For instance if the person seeking admission is a member of a family already in Canada, financially responsible and capable of giving satisfactory security against such an immigrant becoming a public charge, in such a case there would appear to be sufficient justification to relax the regulations to enable that person to join his family. On the other hand, a person with no family ties in Canada would most likely become a public charge, and a rather serious one. The amount involved would run into thousands of dollars for each person.
Another point on which I would like to make an observation is that other departments of government, besides that of manpower and immigration, are particularly concerned, such as the Department of National Health and Welfare on the medical side, and the Department of Justice with regard to legal

consideration of this bill. They should express their views on the bill.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the intent of Bill C-10 is certainly commendable. It is the sort of measure that one can gladly support, but it could profit by amendments that would widen its scope. We should be certain that it is acceptable, from the medical and legal point of view, by those departments of the federal government that are also concerned with its application.

Mr. Speaker, it is with much pleasure that I lend my support to this bill. I express our gratitude to the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) for introducing it. It is a very minute bill but it is of much importance to a lot of people.
I have listened with much interest to the very eloquent speech just made by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) and I gather from those remarks, from one who is interested in the whole problem of mental retardation and our responsibility in society to those so afflicted, that here is a gentleman who does have a concern and also an in-depth knowledge of the problem. I commend him for the remarks he made. However, I find it difficult to understand his reasoning in asking that this bill be set aside for the purpose of expanding it to meet other inadequacies in the immigration law, because to open the whole Immigration Act, even to this problem, is something that goes far beyond the scope of Bill C-10. Therefore I would urge him to reconsider his stand and look at Bill C-10 for what it actually says.
The bill is intended to make it possible for parents who have retarded children in their families to bring those children to this country in the same way as they are able to bring their other children. The bill is even so cautious as to specify that the parents must be able to guarantee that there is support for such children.
Let me be specific. I know of at least three cases, and I am thinking of one in particular, of families having a very real problem because our immigration laws do not permit a child suffering from mental retardation to have the normal status of his brothers and sisters in this country. The particular case I have in mind is that of a professional man. He came to this country, well qualified, a few years ago, but he has to go back to the immigration people year by year to receive a permit to allow his only child, who happens to be retarded, to stay here in Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. C-10 is to provide that a person afflicted with mental retardation may be admitted to Canada under the Immigration Act if he is not likely to become a public charge. In other words, the absolute prohibition against such a person would be relaxed to the degree applicable to persons who are dumb, blind or otherwise physically defective. To accomplish the objective, the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) proposes to repeal paragraph (s) of section 5 of the Immigration Act which prohibits the admission of the following individuals:
Parsons, not included in any other prohibited class, who are certified by a medical officer as being mentally or physically abnormal to such a degree as to impair seriously their ability to earn a living.
The sponsor would substitute:
Persons, not included in any other prohibited class, who are certified by a medical officer as being mentally or physically abnormal to such a degree as to impair seriously their ability to earn a living, unless, where such persons are abnormal by reason of mental retardation.
(i)	they have sufficient means of support or such profession, trade, occupation, employment or other legitimate mode of earning a living that they are not likely to become public charges, or
(ii)	they are members of a family accompanying or already in Canada and the family gives satisfactory security against such immigrants becoming public charges.
I am certain the hon. member has proposed his amendment with the best of intentions. I think we all agree that its expressed objective is a commendable one. I cannot, however, support Bill C-10 since unfortunately it would not accomplish the intended purpose.

My hon. friend proposes to amend section 5(s) of the Immigration Act as a means of facilitating the admission of the mentally retarded. I think, however, he has misunderstood the nature of section 5(s). By including section 5(s) in the Immigration Act parliament provided a discretionary power which can be used under very limited circumstances and only on the basis of a medical certification. Section 5(s) is a residual section. It covers individuals not included in any
[Mr. Thompson (Red Deer) .1

other prohibited class. It cannot be applied without medical certification. A certification can only be made if an individual is mentally or physically abnormal "to such a degree as to impair seriously their ability to earn a living".
Because of the restrictions contained in section 5(s) it is rarely used. As a matter of fact it was used on only two occasions in 1965, five occasions in 1966 and six occasions in 1967. If the mentally retarded are prohibited, it is usually because their retardation is so severe as to place them within section 5(a)(i) of the act which absolutely prohibits the admission of idiots, imbeciles and morons whether they wish to come to Canada as immigrants or non-immigrants. The amendment proposed by my hon. friend would neither remove nor relax that prohibition. Hence its passage would give only the semblance of a relaxation on behalf of those unfortunates who are mentally retarded.
I think the members of this house will agree that the absolute prohibition on the admission of those who suffer severe mental retardation probably accurately reflects the views which were prevalent some 15 years ago when the present Immigration Act was passed. But I think it will be generally agreed that it does not reflect today's attitudes. The previous minister and the present minister relaxed the absolute prohibition on the admission of those afflicted with mental retardation by using the authority provided by parliament, and allowed them to enter under ministers' permits. In 1966, there were 65 ministers' permits issued allowing the admission of such persons. In 1967, we see that 72 were issued, while 56 were issued during the first nine months of 1968.
This of course is a temporary solution. The white paper gives a clear indication of this government's opinion that substantial changes are desirable in the existing statutory grounds for prohibiting the admission of people to Canada. These changes would include a removal of the absolute prohibition on those afflicted by severe mental retardation. As indicated in paragraph 58, page 25 of the white paper, which the hon. member for Surrey read when he was speaking, they would be prohibited only if they represented a danger to society or were not assured of private care.
The views contained in the white paper will be reflected in the new immigration act. Until that act is passed we shall continue to provide relief through the use of ministers''

permits. The need for this practice would not be removed by the passage of Bill C-10 because, as I hope hon. members now realize, this bill would not in effect relax the present statutory prohibition against the mentally retarded.
In summary, may I say that I appreciate and share the desire of the sponsor of this bill to facilitate the admission of the mentally retarded by amending the act. I cannot however support his bill since it would not accomplish that objective but indeed might raise false hopes.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Surrey some changes should be made in this act concerning the rules. In article 63(b) of the white paper we find that the following type of person would be prohibited:
A mentally or physically defective person unless he is a member of a family otherwise admissible and well able to look after him.
So, this is clear-cut in the white paper on immigration of 1966, when this white paper is acted upon.
